title: Basil and the Sky Puddle
markdown:
Once upon a time, way up high in the Twinkletop Hills, where the clouds sometimes tickled the mountain tops like sleepy giants yawning, there lived a little wizard named Basil. Basil had eyes as bright and blue as two tiny blueberries that had just been picked, and his hair was the colour of toast that had been toasted just right – golden and cozy. He was a wizard, you see, a proper little wizard, but he was still learning. Sometimes his potions would fizzle and pop like popcorn. And other times his magic wands would do a little wiggle-waggle all on their own, like they were trying to tell a joke. It was all very enthusiastic. But Basil was a very kind wizard. And he had the bestest friend in the whole wide world, a crow named Corvus.

Every single day, as sure as the sun peeked over the mountains like a shy peekaboo player, Basil would tiptoe into the most wonderful place: the tinkling fir grove. Oh, this grove. The pine needles there whispered secrets to the breeze – shhh, shhh – and the air always smelled like a warm cozy Christmas morning, even in the middle of summer. Basil would hold up his special wand, a shimmery thing he had found that looked like a fallen moonbeam. He would wave it with a flourish – whoosh – and try out his newest most exciting charms. “Abracadabra… twinkle toes.” He hoped his boots would start tap-dancing. But usually, instead of dancing boots, his shoelaces would tie themselves into the neatest little bows. They probably wanted to win a fashion show. And that would make Corvus let out the happiest most excited caw you ever did hear. Caw-caw-caw. Corvus was a crow with feathers as black and shiny as a polished midnight stone. He would perch on a low-hanging branch, his beady eyes watching Basil with so much care and attention. He was a truly excellent crow, a wonderfully watchful crow, and he really, really did not like getting his feet wet. Not one single teeny-tiny drop. He would shake his tail feathers like he was trying to dry off after swimming in a teapot.

Until one sunshiny day, Basil and Corvus decided to be a little bit brave. They wandered a bit deeper into the fir grove than they usually did, past the whispering trees and the Christmas-smelling air. The trees here were even taller, their branches stretching out like sleepy giant arms reaching for the sky. Corvus, who was always the first to notice something new (he had super-duper crow eyes, you know), suddenly stopped. His little head tilted, and he let out a curious caw. His beak pointed down, down, down, towards something that was shimmering, sparkling, and glistening on the ground. Basil, a little wizard’s robe swishing around his knees like a happy skirt, peered where Corvus was looking. And oh, my goodness gracious. It was a puddle. But this was not just any ordinary muddy puddle. This puddle was amazing. It looked exactly, precisely, wonderfully, like the sky. It was a perfect bright blue, and there were fluffy white clouds floating right there on the dirt, as if the sky had decided to take a little nap on the ground.

“Wowee,” whispered Basil, his eyes wide. Corvus, for just a moment, forgot all about his dislike of wet feet. He was so incredibly curious. He hopped forward, his little crow feet twitching, looking as if he might just dive right in for a friendly wave to the sky-clouds. Oh dear.

“Whoa, Corvus, wait a minute, hold your feathers.” Basil’s voice sounded a little like a squeaky mouse who had just stubbed his toe. He remembered how Corvus would puff up his chest and do a whole jig of flapping and shaking if even a single speck of water dared to touch his toes. Basil knelt down so he was closer to his friend. His long big wizard robes made a gentle rustling sound, like leaves dancing. “That is a super-duper nice sky, Corvus.” He held out his hand, not to grab Corvus, but just to show him the way to go. “Come on, my brave crow. Let’s go this way. We do not want your beautiful shiny feathers to get all puddle-y and soggy.” Corvus blinked his intelligent beady eyes, then gave a little shake of his head, a soft caw-caw that sounded like he agreed. He hopped closer to Basil, right beside his outstretched hand, and together they turned away from the tempting sky-puddle, their little adventure taking a new turn.

Because of that wonderful decision, they wandered a little bit further, their feet making a soft crunching sound on the fallen leaves. The tall fir trees started to get a little less crowded, and the warm sunlight dappled through the leaves, making little golden puddles dance on the forest floor. And then Basil heard it. A sound like distant rumbling thunder, but so, so much gentler. It sounded like a giant sleepy bear snoring, but a happy snoring, full of warm sunshine.

“Caw?” Corvus chirped, and he fluttered up to perch on Basil’s shoulder, his tiny sharp claws tickling through the thick fabric of Basil’s robe. He was curious again.

Basil carefully peeked through the last few trees. And oh, what a sight met his eyes. Standing in a bright patch of warm sunshine, carefully nudging a fluffy white sheep with a very, very large, but surprisingly gentle, clumsy hand, was an ogre. But this was not a grumpy stompy ogre from one of those less-than-happy stories. This ogre had a beard that was as green and soft as the moss that grew on the old stones, and his eyes crinkled up at the corners like happy little crescents when he looked at his fluffy sheep. He wore a tunic made of all sorts of colourful patches sewn together, and he was humming a low rumbling tune that sounded just like the wind sighing through the mountaintops.

The ogre looked up, his big kind eyes finding Basil and Corvus. He did not roar, and he did not stomp his big feet. Instead he smiled, a wide warm smile that showed a few teeth that were a little bit crooked, but perfectly friendly. “Well, hello there, little wizard. And hello to your very fine feathered friend. My name is Crumble.”

Basil, feeling a little shy but also very, very curious, waved a small hand. “Hello, Crumble. I am Basil, and this is my best friend, Corvus.”

Crumble chuckled, a sound like happy gravel being stirred. “Corvus, you say? A very fine name for such a watchful crow. What brings you all the way out here to my hillside?”

Basil, feeling more brave now that Crumble was so nice, explained about their walk and the amazing sky-puddle, and how Corvus had almost, almost hopped right in. Crumble’s crinkly eyes twinkled with understanding. “Ah, the sky-puddle. You know, little wizard, that puddle is not the sky at all. It is just the sky looking down at us from the water. It is a reflection.”

Because of that wonderful simple explanation, Basil looked back towards where they had come from. And Crumble was absolutely, positively right. The puddle was just a mirror, a special watery mirror showing them the beautiful vast blue sky above. Basil felt a little flutter of understanding bloom in his wizard’s heart, like a tiny seed of knowing pushing through the soil. He was so busy trying to make his own magic with his wand and spells, he had not stopped to truly see the magic that was already all around them, in the sky, and on the ground. He felt proud of himself for gently coaxing Corvus away from the tempting sky-puddle, but even prouder of Crumble for showing him a new quiet kind of wonder.

Crumble then gently explained that the sky-puddle was a perfect example of looking closely. He said that sometimes things are not quite what they first seem, and it is always a good idea to have kind friends to help you see them clearly. Corvus, still perched on Basil’s shoulder, gave a soft contented caw, as if to say yes, yes, I understand perfectly. And Crumble’s fluffy sheep, all soft and woolly, let out contented little bleats, as if agreeing with everything Crumble said.

Until finally, as the sun began to dip lower, painting the sky in streaks of warm orange and soft pink, Crumble invited Basil and Corvus to sit with him for a moment. They settled down on the soft mossy ground. Basil leaned his head back against a large warm rock, feeling cozy and safe. Corvus snuggled into Basil’s neck, a warm feathery weight that felt like a hug. They sat there, just being, and watched as the last rays of sunlight filtered through the tall fir trees, making the whole world shimmer with a gentle golden glow. It was a quiet beautiful moment, filled with the fresh smell of pine needles and damp earth, and the soft sounds of the countryside sighing. There was no need for magic words or grand spells. Just the simple perfect peace of being together, sharing the quiet beauty of the world.

Ever since that wonderful day, Basil and Corvus have kept walking the Twinkletop Hills. They still practise their spells, and sometimes, yes, they still tie their shoelaces into bows by accident. The sky-puddle stays on the path, blue and cloudy. Corvus still hops around it. His feet stay dry.
characters: Basil (young wizard with toast-coloured hair), Corvus (a watchful crow who hates wet feet)
